title: Strong vs eventual consistency
description: Learn the difference between strong and eventual consistency models. Understand when to use each and their trade-offs.

data.text: Consistency models define how and when data becomes visible across replicas in a distributed system. Strong consistency guarantees that all reads see the most recent write, while eventual consistency only guarantees that replicas will converge over time.
Strong consistency (also called linearizability) ensures that every read returns the most recent write or an error. The system behaves as if there were a single copy of the data.

items: All nodes see the same data at the same time
No stale reads—guarantees freshness
Requires coordination between replicas
Higher latency due to synchronization overhead
Lower availability during network partitions (CAP theorem)

data.title: When to Use
data.text: Strong consistency is essential for financial transactions, inventory management, authentication, and any system where incorrect data could cause serious problems.
Eventual consistency guarantees that if no new updates are made, eventually all accesses will return the last updated value. Replicas may return stale data temporarily but will converge.

items: Replicas may diverge temporarily
Reads may return stale data
No coordination required for reads—fast performance
High availability even during partitions
Convergence time varies (milliseconds to minutes)

data.title: When to Use
data.text: Eventual consistency works well for social media feeds, caching layers, analytics, and systems where slight staleness is acceptable.

items.title: Strong Consistency
items.description: Pros: Correct data, simpler reasoning, ACID transactions. Cons: Higher latency, lower availability, harder to scale geographically.

items.title: Eventual Consistency
items.description: Pros: Low latency, high availability, easy scaling. Cons: Stale reads, complex reasoning, harder to debug inconsistencies.

data.text: Consistency isn't binary—there's a spectrum between strong and eventual.

items: Strong (linearizable)—strict ordering, highest guarantees
Causal consistency—preserves cause-effect relationships
Session consistency—guarantees within a user session
Read-your-writes—you always see your own writes
Eventual—only guarantees convergence eventually

data.text: When using eventual consistency, you need patterns to handle the temporary inconsistencies.

items: Version vectors or vector clocks to track causality
Conflict resolution strategies (last-write-wins, application-specific merging)
Read repair—detect and fix inconsistencies during reads
Anti-entropy processes—background synchronization
Quorum reads/writes to bound inconsistency

data.title: Watch Out
data.text: Don't assume eventual consistency is always faster. Poorly designed conflict resolution can be expensive and slow. Consider your read/write patterns carefully.
Start by understanding your business requirements.

items: What's the cost of showing stale data? If high, use strong consistency
What's the cost of being unavailable? If high, consider eventual consistency
What's your geographic distribution? Strong consistency gets harder with distance
What's your read/write ratio? Eventual consistency benefits read-heavy workloads
Can you implement application-level conflict resolution?
